newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German March industry orders.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German March industry orders.

text.p: Following are reactions of economists to data which showed an increase in Pan-German industry orders of 1.1 percent in March against February.
Orders rose in western Germany by 0.7 percent, but were up by a sharp 7.4 percent in the formerly-communist east.

"The orders rise was stronger than expected, it now looks as if for the first quarter of 1997 orders will be up 1.5 percent from the previous quarter. That is fairly positive and we think gross domestic product for the first quarter will definitely be up 0.5 percent from the previous quarter, possibly even more.

But we are seeing mixed signals. Output looks favourable but the labour situation is disappointing, the jobs data this morning were worse than expected and the seasonal improvement in the jobs market was weaker than seen in previous years. Exports are the driving force for the economy, not domestic demand."

"The orders data were much stronger than expected and they confirm that the economy is growing faster than generally expected, particularly in the industrial sector. We're seeing strong demand from within Germany, especially for investment goods and we're seeing that the domestic investment cycle is beginning to pick up. "But domestic demand for consumer goods remains weak.

"I see first quarter GDP rising by 0.7 or 0.8 percent from the previous quarter and there will be a clear acceleration in the second quarter, with growth likely to be about one percent. I don't have to revise my full-year forecast for GDP growth because that is three percent, above the consensus."

"These are similar to the industrial production numbers yesterday, and indicate a further slight advance in the recovery in both east and west Germany. The economy is gaining, step-by-step, although it is hard going."

The orders data, a leading indicator, will not feed through into an early fall in joblessness after seasonally-adjusted data earlier showed a small rise for April, Pietsch said. "We expect unemployment, a lagging indicator, to fall in the second half of the year."

On the prospects for cutting government borrowing to qualify for European monetary union: "I am still very optimistic that Germany can achieve the deficit criterion. Although the next tax estimates will be weak, only small savings will be needed. In the second half of the year the federal government and the states should be able to put together the necessary savings."
